items.title: Quiz Q#1 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Match List I (Modern Novel) with List II (Shakespeare's Play from which its title was taken):
List I:
(A) Pale Fire (Vladimir Nabokov)
(B) Cakes and Ale (W. Somerset Maugham)
(C) Brave New World (Aldous Huxley)
(D) Under the Greenwood Tree (Thomas Hardy)

List II:
(I) Twelfth Night
(II) Timon of Athens
(III) As You Like It
(IV) The Tempest

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Nabokov's Pale Fire (1962) comes from Timon of Athens ('the moon's an arrant thief, / And her pale fire she snatches from the sun'). Maugham's Cakes and Ale (1930) comes from Sir Toby Belch's line in Twelfth Night. Huxley's Brave New World (1932) comes from Miranda's speech in The Tempest. Hardy's Under the Greenwood Tree (1872) comes from Amiens' song in As You Like It.

items.title: Quiz Q#2 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Match List I (Critic) with List II (Critical View on Shakespeare):
List I:
(A) Samuel Pepys
(B) Thomas Rymer
(C) Samuel Taylor Coleridge
(D) T. S. Eliot

List II:
(I) Described Iago's soliloquies in Othello as 'the motive-hunting of motiveless malignity'
(II) Called A Midsummer Night's Dream 'the most insipid ridiculous play that ever I saw in my life'
(III) Declared Hamlet 'most certainly an artistic failure' and praised Coriolanus and Antony and Cleopatra
(IV) Attacked Othello as a farce with a moral warning wives to 'look well to their Linen'

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In his 1662 diary, Samuel Pepys dismissed A Midsummer Night's Dream as 'the most insipid ridiculous play'. Thomas Rymer mocked Othello in A Short View of Tragedy (1693). S. T. Coleridge coined 'motiveless malignity' for Iago. T. S. Eliot called Hamlet an 'artistic failure' in Hamlet and His Problems (1919).

items.title: Quiz Q#3 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Arrange the following plays of William Shakespeare in the chronological order of their composition:
(A) The Tempest
(B) The Comedy of Errors
(C) Julius Caesar
(D) Macbeth
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Comedy of Errors is one of Shakespeare's earliest farcical comedies (c. 1589-1594). Julius Caesar was written and performed in 1599 (at the newly opened Globe Theatre). Macbeth is a Jacobean tragedy from 1606. The Tempest (1610-1611) is his final solo romance.

items.title: Quiz Q#4 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The First Folio of Shakespeare's plays (1623), compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell, included 36 plays but omitted Pericles, Prince of Tyre and The Two Noble Kinsmen.
Statement II: John Milton's poem 'On Shakespeare' (composed 1630) was first printed in the First Folio of 1623.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Statement I is true: the 1623 First Folio contained 36 plays and omitted Pericles and The Two Noble Kinsmen. Statement II is false because John Milton was only 14 years old in 1623; his poem 'On Shakespeare' was composed in 1630 and printed in the Second Folio of 1632.

items.title: Quiz Q#7 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Which of the following statements about Shakespeare's Sonnets (1609) are correct?
(A) They were published in Quarto in 1609 by Thomas Thorpe with a dedication to 'Mr. W. H.'
(B) The first 17 sonnets are known as the 'Procreation Sonnets'
(C) Sonnets 127 to 152 are addressed to the 'Dark Lady'
(D) Sonnet 99 contains 15 lines, while Sonnet 126 contains 12 lines in rhyming couplets
(E) All 154 sonnets follow the Petrarchan octave-sestet rhyme scheme
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Statements (A), (B), (C), and (D) are all true. Statement (E) is false because Shakespeare used the English (Surreyan/Shakespearean) sonnet form consisting of three quatrains and a final rhyming couplet (abab cdcd efef gg), not the Italian Petrarchan octave-sestet form.

items.title: Quiz Q#8 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In which play of Shakespeare does the ancient English poet John Gower appear on stage as the Chorus to introduce each act with a Prologue and deliver the Epilogue?
items.explanation: In Pericles, Prince of Tyre (whose plot is drawn partly from John Gower's 1393 poem Confessio Amantis), Gower himself appears as the Chorus/Narrator before every act and speaks the closing Epilogue. (In Henry IV Part 2, 'Rumour' speaks the Prologue; in The Winter's Tale, 'Time' appears as Chorus before Act IV).

items.title: Quiz Q#9 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): In his 1765 Preface to Shakespeare, Dr. Samuel Johnson defended Shakespeare for violating the dramatic unities of time and place.
Reason (R): Johnson argued that spectators are always in their senses and know from the first act to the last that the stage is only a stage and the players are only players.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: While Dr. Johnson respected the Unity of Action, he demolished the neoclassical insistence on the Unities of Time and Place by pointing out that audiences never literally believe they are in Alexandria in Act I; therefore, their imagination can easily move from Alexandria to Rome in Act II.

items.title: Quiz Q#10 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Who rewrote Shakespeare's King Lear in 1681 with a happy ending in which Cordelia survives and marries Edgar, a version that held the English stage for 150 years?
items.explanation: In 1681, Restoration poet laureate Nahum Tate adapted King Lear with a happy ending where Lear regains his throne and Cordelia marries Edgar (omitting the Fool entirely). Even Dr. Samuel Johnson defended Tate's happy ending because he found Cordelia's death in Shakespeare's original too painful to read.

items.title: Quiz Q#11 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost (Act 5, Scene 1), which clownish character utters the 27-letter Latin word 'Honorificabilitudinitatibus', the longest word in all of Shakespeare's works?
items.explanation: Costard the clown says 'Honorificabilitudinitatibus' (meaning 'the state of being able to achieve honours') to the tiny page Moth while mocking the pedantic Latin of schoolmaster Holofernes and Don Armado.

items.title: Quiz Q#12 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Twelfth Night, what are the four mysterious letters written on the forged love letter dropped by Maria that trick steward Malvolio into wearing yellow stockings and cross-garters?
items.explanation: Maria's forged letter contains the riddle 'M. O. A. I. doth sway my life'. Proud Malvolio convinces himself that those four letters are in his own name (M-A-L-V-O-L-I-O) and follows the letter's ridiculous instructions to wear yellow stockings and smile constantly.

items.title: Quiz Q#13 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In The Merchant of Venice, what inscription is written on the Lead Casket correctly chosen by Bassanio at Belmont?
options: All that glisters is not gold.
Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire.
Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves.
Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath.
items.explanation: Portia's father left three caskets: Gold ('Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire', chosen by the Prince of Morocco), Silver ('Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves', chosen by the Prince of Arragon), and Lead ('Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath', chosen by Bassanio).

items.title: Quiz Q#14 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: What is the name of the poison that Claudius pours into the ears of sleeping King Hamlet in the orchard?
items.explanation: In Act 1 Scene 5 of Hamlet, the Ghost reveals to Prince Hamlet that while he was sleeping in his orchard, his brother Claudius crept up with a vial of 'juice of cursed hebenon' and poured the leprous distilment into the porches of his ears.

items.title: Quiz Q#15 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which character in As You Like It delivers the famous 'Seven Ages of Man' speech beginning 'All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players'?
items.explanation: In Act 2 Scene 7 of As You Like It, the melancholic lord Jaques addresses Duke Senior in the Forest of Arden, dividing human life into seven stages: the infant, the whining schoolboy, the lover, the soldier, the justice, the lean and slippered pantaloon, and second childishness ('Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything').

items.explanation: Colloquies (1518) is Erasmus's celebrated collection of lively Latin dialogues touching on religious reform, superstition, and social customs.

items.title: Quiz Q#107 · Desiderius Erasmus
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Desiderius Erasmus
items.stem: Which work by Desiderius Erasmus began as a modest phrasebook of Latin conversational greetings before growing across multiple editions into a renowned compendium of humanist satire?
items.explanation: Erasmus's Colloquies (1518/19) evolved over many years into a wide-ranging critique of contemporary ecclesiastical abuses, scholasticism, and superstition.

items.title: Quiz Q#108 · Desiderius Erasmus
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Desiderius Erasmus
items.stem: In which satirical masterpiece by Desiderius Erasmus does the personification of Folly (Stultitia) deliver an ironic encomium praising human foolishness and vanity?
items.explanation: In Praise of Folly (Moriae Encomium, 1511), Folly personified delivers an ironic oration exposing the pretensions of theologians, monks, popes, and kings.

items.title: Quiz Q#109 · Desiderius Erasmus
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Desiderius Erasmus
items.stem:

"I, Folly, am the only one"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Desiderius Erasmus's Praise of Folly (1511).

items.title: Quiz Q#110 · Desiderius Erasmus
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Desiderius Erasmus
items.stem: Which satirical work by Desiderius Erasmus, written in 1509 while staying at the home of Sir Thomas More, bears the Latin title Moriae Encomium?
items.explanation: Praise of Folly (Moriae Encomium, 1511) was dedicated to Erasmus's dear friend Sir Thomas More, playing on More's surname and the Greek word for folly ('moria').

items.title: Quiz Q#111 · Thomas More
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas More
items.stem: In which landmark 1516 philosophical dialogue by Sir Thomas More does the traveler Raphael Hythloday describe the communal laws and customs of an ideal island commonwealth?
items.explanation: Raphael Hythloday narrates the customs of the ideal society in Sir Thomas More's Utopia (1516), coining the Greek term for 'no-place'.

items.title: Quiz Q#112 · Thomas More
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas More

items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas More
items.stem: Which seminal humanist work by Sir Thomas More, originally printed in Latin at Leuven in 1516, was translated into English by Ralph Robinson in 1551?
items.explanation: Sir Thomas More's Utopia was published in Latin in 1516; Ralph Robinson produced the first English vernacular translation in 1551.

items.title: Quiz Q#114 · Thomas Elyot
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Elyot
items.stem: Which 1531 educational treatise by Sir Thomas Elyot was designed to train young Tudor aristocrats in statesmanship, classical virtues, and physical exercises like dancing and archery?
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Elyot's The Book Named the Governor (1531) is the earliest work on moral philosophy and statesmanship published in the English vernacular.

items.title: Quiz Q#115 · Thomas Elyot
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Elyot

items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Elyot
items.stem: Which 1531 work, dedicated to King Henry VIII and printed by Thomas Berthelet, sought to augment the English vocabulary with loanwords while establishing a humanist curriculum for rulers?
items.explanation: The Book Named the Governor (1531) by Sir Thomas Elyot introduced classical concepts into English governance and enriched the vernacular vocabulary.

items.title: Quiz Q#117 · William Tyndale
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Tyndale
items.stem:

items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Tyndale's English New Testament (1526).

items.title: Quiz Q#118 · William Tyndale
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Tyndale
items.stem: Which translation by William Tyndale, printed in Germany in 1526, served as the first English scripture translated directly from original Greek manuscripts?
items.explanation: William Tyndale's English New Testament (1526) was translated directly from Erasmus's Greek text and formed the foundation for the King James Bible of 1611.

items.title: Quiz Q#119 · William Tyndale
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Tyndale
items.stem: Which translation project by William Tyndale, printed at Antwerp in 1530 under the pseudonym of Hans Luft in Marburg, rendered Genesis through Deuteronomy into English directly from Hebrew?
items.explanation: William Tyndale's Pentateuch translation (1530) marked the first time the first five books of the Old Testament were translated directly from Hebrew into English.

items.title: Quiz Q#120 · Thomas Wyatt
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Wyatt
items.stem: Which collection of poems by Sir Thomas Wyatt, posthumously published in Tottel's Miscellany (1557), introduced the Petrarchan sonnet structure and courtly love conceits into English literature?
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Wyatt's Sonnets after Petrarch adapted Petrarch's Italian sonnets into English, pioneering the fourteen-line form alongside the Earl of Surrey.

items.title: Quiz Q#122 · Thomas Wyatt
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Wyatt
items.stem: Which landmark collection of Renaissance poetry circulated in manuscript during the author's lifetime before being published by Richard Tottel in Songes and Sonettes (1557)?
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Wyatt's Sonnets after Petrarch circulated among Henrician courtiers and were first printed fifteen years after his death in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).

items.title: Quiz Q#123 · Thomas Wyatt
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Wyatt
items.stem: In which famous lyric poem by Sir Thomas Wyatt does the speaker lament that former courtly lovers who once sought him in his chamber now 'range / Busily seeking with a continual change'?
items.explanation: 'They Flee from Me' is Sir Thomas Wyatt's celebrated rhyme royal lyric meditating on the mutability and fickle affections of courtly love.

items.explanation: 'They Flee from Me' circulated widely in manuscript before Richard Tottel regularized its rhythm and published it in Songes and Sonettes (1557).

items.title: Quiz Q#126 · Thomas Wyatt
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Wyatt

items.explanation: Wyatt's 'Whoso List to Hunt' adapts Petrarch's deer allegory into English vernacular sonnet form, lamenting the futility of chasing Caesar's hind.

items.explanation: The Scholemaster (1570), published posthumously by Roger Ascham's widow Margaret, is a classic humanist guide to teaching Latin through gentle discipline.

items.explanation: In The Scholemaster (1570), Roger Ascham famously warns against sending young English scholars to Italy, quoting the Italian proverb 'Inglese italianato è un diavolo incarnato'.

items.title: Quiz Q#132 · Roger Ascham
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Roger Ascham
items.stem: Which 1545 dialogue by Roger Ascham, written in English to prove the capability of the vernacular, defends archery as both a military duty and scholar's pastime?
items.explanation: Toxophilus (1545), meaning 'lover of the bow', is Roger Ascham's patriotic treatise and dialogue promoting longbow archery in clear English prose.

items.explanation: Toxophilus (1545) was written by Roger Ascham to celebrate English archery and demonstrate that serious scholarly matter could be written in English rather than Latin.

items.title: Quiz Q#135 · Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

items.title: Quiz Q#138 · Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

items.title: Quiz Q#140 · Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

items.title: Quiz Q#142 · Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

items.explanation: The Arte of English Poesie (1589) offered Elizabethan poets practical guidance on meters, stanzaic patterns, ocular verse, and rhetorical tropes.

items.title: Quiz Q#146 · Edmund Spenser

items.title: Quiz Q#149 · Edmund Spenser

items.explanation: The Shepheardes Calender (1579) was Spenser's breakthrough pastoral work, accompanied by the scholarly commentary of the mysterious E.K.

items.title: Quiz Q#152 · Edmund Spenser
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: Which 1595 sonnet sequence of 89 poems by Edmund Spenser celebrates his courtship of Elizabeth Boyle and culminates in Sonnet 75 ('One day I wrote her name upon the strand')?
items.explanation: Amoretti (1595) is Spenser's interlocking-rhyme sonnet sequence (abab bcbc cdcd ee) charting his romantic courtship of his second wife.

items.title: Quiz Q#153 · Edmund Spenser
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Edmund Spenser
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"My verse your vertues rare shall eternize."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Edmund Spenser's Amoretti (1595).

items.title: Quiz Q#154 · Edmund Spenser
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: Which Elizabethan sonnet sequence differs from traditional Petrarchan collections by celebrating successful, reciprocated courtship leading to Christian marriage rather than unattainable love?
items.explanation: Spenser's Amoretti (1595) is unique among Renaissance sonnet cycles for culminating in joyful marital union celebrated in Epithalamion.

items.title: Quiz Q#155 · Edmund Spenser
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: In which 1595 lyric masterpiece does Edmund Spenser act as the joyous bridegroom invoking the nymphs of the river Mulla to grace his wedding day?
items.explanation: In Epithalamion (1595), Spenser celebrates his own wedding to Elizabeth Boyle on midsummer day 1594 in Kilcolman, Ireland.

items.title: Quiz Q#156 · Edmund Spenser
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Edmund Spenser
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Open the temple gates unto my love."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Edmund Spenser's Epithalamion (1595).

items.title: Quiz Q#157 · Edmund Spenser
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: Which 1595 Spenserian ode consists of 24 elaborate stanzas mirroring the 24 hours of midsummer day, concluding with an envoy dedicating the poem as an eternal wedding gift?
items.explanation: Epithalamion (1595) is constructed with intricate temporal symbolism, matching 24 stanzas to the 24 hours of daylight and night on Spenser's wedding day.

items.title: Quiz Q#158 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem: In which 1578 prose romance by John Lyly does a witty young Athenian gentleman travel to Naples and debate moral virtue and fickle love, giving rise to the term 'Euphuism'?
items.explanation: John Lyly's Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578) established the highly stylized, antithetical rhetorical mode that swept Elizabethan court literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#159 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"love, which is lawless"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Lyly's Euphues (1578).

items.title: Quiz Q#160 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem: Which Elizabethan prose work popularized an ornate courtly style characterized by antithetical parallelism, rhetorical questions, alliterative balance, and similes drawn from fabulous natural history?
items.explanation: Euphues (1578) by John Lyly gave its name to Euphuism, the ornate prose style that deeply influenced early Elizabethan writers including Greene and Lodge.

items.title: Quiz Q#161 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem: In which mythological court comedy by John Lyly does the title protagonist fall into a sleep of forty years on a bank of lunary because of his devoted adoration of Cynthia, Queen of the Moon?
items.explanation: Endymion, the Man in the Moon (1591) by John Lyly allegorizes courtly devotion to Queen Elizabeth through the classical myth of Cynthia and Endymion.

items.title: Quiz Q#162 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem: Which court comedy by John Lyly was performed before Queen Elizabeth at Greenwich by the Children of Paul's, weaving an elaborate courtly allegory involving Tellus, Eumenides, and Cynthia?
items.explanation: Lyly's Endymion (1591) is a celebrated example of Elizabethan courtly drama written for boy actors, offering flattering allegorical tribute to Queen Elizabeth.

items.title: Quiz Q#163 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem: In which pastoral comedy by John Lyly do two maidens, Gallathea and Phillida, both disguise themselves as boys to escape sacrifice to Neptune's sea monster, and unwittingly fall in love with each other?
items.explanation: John Lyly's Gallathea (1592) features two cross-dressed heroines whose mutual romantic affection is resolved when Venus promises to transform one into a boy.

items.title: Quiz Q#164 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I will never love any but Phillida."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Lyly's Gallathea (1592).

items.title: Quiz Q#165 · John Lyly
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Lyly
items.stem: Which mythological pastoral play by John Lyly directly influenced Shakespeare's romantic comedies through its sophisticated exploration of female cross-dressing, pastoral retreat, and Cupid's mischievous arrows?
items.explanation: Gallathea (1592) served as a vital dramaturgical model for Shakespeare's romantic comedies, particularly As You Like It and Twelfth Night.

items.title: Quiz Q#166 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem: In which seminal critical treatise does Sir Philip Sidney defend imaginative literature against Stephen Gosson's Puritan attacks, arguing that 'the poet never maketh any circles about your imagination, to conjure you to believe for true what he writes'?
items.explanation: The Defence of Poesy (An Apology for Poetry, 1595) was Sidney's reply to Gosson's School of Abuse, arguing that poetry teaches and delights better than history or philosophy.

items.title: Quiz Q#167 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The poet nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Philip Sidney's The Defence of Poesy (1595).

items.title: Quiz Q#168 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem: Which 1595 Renaissance critical manifesto by Sir Philip Sidney, published posthumously in rival editions by William Ponsonby and Henry Olney, championed poetry as a creative imitation superior to philosophy and history?
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney's critical essay was published posthumously in 1595 as both The Defence of Poesie (Ponsonby) and An Apologie for Poetrie (Olney).

items.title: Quiz Q#169 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem: In Sir Philip Sidney's pastoral romance Arcadia, which prince disguises himself as the Amazon warrior Zelmane to gain access to King Basilius' sequestered daughter Philoclea?
items.explanation: In Sidney's Arcadia (1590), Prince Pyrocles disguises himself as the Amazon Zelmane, while his companion Musidorus disguises himself as the shepherd Dorus.

items.title: Quiz Q#170 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"What tongue can her perfections tell."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Philip Sidney's Arcadia (1590, composite edition 1593).

items.title: Quiz Q#171 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem: Which monumental Elizabethan prose romance was originally composed by Sir Philip Sidney for the entertainment of his sister Mary Herbert, Countess of Pembroke, and left in both 'Old' and 'New' versions?
items.explanation: The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia exists as Sidney's original manuscript romance (Old Arcadia, c. 1580) and his elaborate revised epic version (New Arcadia, 1590).

items.title: Quiz Q#172 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem: In which pioneering 1591 English sonnet sequence does the speaker Astrophil passionately court his beloved Stella (widely identified as Lady Penelope Devereux)?
items.explanation: Astrophil and Stella (1591) by Sir Philip Sidney is England's first full sonnet sequence, comprising 108 sonnets and 11 songs detailing the lover's anguish.

items.title: Quiz Q#173 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Look in thy heart, and write."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Philip Sidney's Astrophil and Stella (1591, authorised 1598).

items.title: Quiz Q#174 · Philip Sidney
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Philip Sidney
items.stem: Which 1591 sonnet sequence by Sir Philip Sidney, printed piratically by Thomas Newman before appearing authorized in the 1598 Arcadia folio, sparked the Elizabethan sonnet craze?
items.explanation: The 1591 publication of Astrophil and Stella ignited a decade-long craze for sonnet sequences across Elizabethan England (Spenser, Daniel, Drayton, Shakespeare).

items.title: Quiz Q#175 · Richard Hooker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Richard Hooker
items.stem: Which monumental work of Anglican theological prose by Richard Hooker establishes the 'threefold cord' of Scripture, Reason, and Tradition to defend the Church of England against Presbyterian Puritanism?
options: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity
items.explanation: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (1593) by Richard Hooker is the theological foundation of the Anglican Via Media (Middle Way).

items.title: Quiz Q#176 · Richard Hooker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Richard Hooker
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"her seat is the bosom of God"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Richard Hooker's Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (1593).

items.title: Quiz Q#177 · Richard Hooker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Richard Hooker
items.stem: Which multi-volume theological masterpiece by Richard Hooker, published between 1593 and 1662, defends the ecclesiastical hierarchy, liturgy, and royal supremacy of the English Church through natural law?
options: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity
items.explanation: Hooker's Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity articulated the philosophical defense of the Elizabethan religious settlement against Puritan demands for reform.

items.title: Quiz Q#178 · George Peele
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Peele
items.stem: Which 1599 biblical tragedy by University Wit George Peele dramatizes King David's adulterous love for Bathsheba, the murder of Uriah, and the tragic rebellion of Absalom?
items.explanation: David and Bethsabe (1599) by George Peele is one of the few Elizabethan tragedies drawn directly from Hebrew Scripture, noted for its lyrical blank verse.

items.title: Quiz Q#179 · George Peele
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Peele
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Hot sun, cool fire, tempered with sweet air."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in George Peele's David and Bethsabe (1599).

items.title: Quiz Q#180 · George Peele
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Peele
items.stem: Which poetic drama by George Peele, published in 1599 as 'The Love of King David and Fair Bethsabe', is renowned for its lush pastoral and biblical imagery, including the opening song 'Hot sun, cool fire'?
items.explanation: George Peele's David and Bethsabe (1599) features the famous lyrical opening hymn sung by Bethsabe as she bathes in a spring.

items.title: Quiz Q#181 · George Peele
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Peele
items.stem: In which experimental romantic play by George Peele does the cottager Madge narrate a bedtime fairy tale that comes to life on stage, featuring the Ghost of Jack and the Wandering Knight Erestus?
items.explanation: The Old Wives' Tale (1595) by George Peele is an innovative play-within-a-play parodying chivalric romance and English folklore.

items.title: Quiz Q#182 · George Peele
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Peele
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"When as the rye reach to the chin."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in George Peele's The Old Wives’ Tale (1595).

items.title: Quiz Q#183 · George Peele
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Peele
items.stem: Which 1595 comedy by George Peele is celebrated as a dramatic satire on chivalric romances, incorporating folklore motifs like the Grateful Dead and the Well of Life?
items.explanation: The Old Wives' Tale (1595) influenced Milton's Comus and served as an early English theatrical parody of popular folktales and wandering chivalry.

items.title: Quiz Q#184 · Robert Greene
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Greene
items.stem: In which Elizabethan comedy by Robert Greene does the English scholar Friar Bacon construct a magical Brazen Head that can utter only 'Time is', 'Time was', and 'Time is past'?
items.explanation: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay (1594) by Robert Greene pairs the comic necromancy of Roger Bacon with the pastoral romance of Margaret, the Fair Maid of Fressingfield.

items.title: Quiz Q#185 · Robert Greene
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Greene
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Time is, Time was, Time is past."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Robert Greene's Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay (1594).

items.title: Quiz Q#186 · Robert Greene
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Greene
items.stem: Which 1594 comedy by Robert Greene dramatizes a contest of magical skill between Friar Bacon of Oxford and the German sorcerer Vandermast before King Henry III and the Emperor?
items.explanation: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay (1594) contrasted patriotic English magic with foreign sorcery, proving a rival hit to Marlowe's Doctor Faustus.

items.title: Quiz Q#187 · Robert Greene
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Greene
items.stem: In which pastoral prose romance by Robert Greene does the jealous King Pandosto of Bohemia wrongfully accuse his queen Bellaria of infidelity, leading to the abandonment of their baby daughter Fawnia?
items.explanation: Robert Greene's Pandosto: The Triumph of Time (1588) provided the complete narrative source for Shakespeare's late romance The Winter's Tale.

items.title: Quiz Q#188 · Robert Greene
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Greene
items.stem: Which 1588 prose romance by Robert Greene, subtitled The Triumph of Time, served as the direct source for Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale, although Shakespeare famously swapped the settings of Bohemia and Sicily?
items.explanation: Pandosto (1588) was Greene's best-selling prose romance; Shakespeare drew Leontes, Hermione, Perdita, and Florizel directly from Pandosto, Bellaria, Fawnia, and Dorastus.

items.title: Quiz Q#189 · Thomas Kyd
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Kyd
items.stem: In which pioneering Elizabethan revenge tragedy by Thomas Kyd does the distraught Knight Marshal Hieronimo stage the play Soliman and Perseda to avenge his murdered son Horatio?
items.explanation: The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587-92) by Thomas Kyd established the revenge tragedy genre, complete with a ghost, a play-within-a-play, feigned madness, and bloody retribution.

items.title: Quiz Q#190 · Thomas Kyd
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Kyd
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Hieronimo is mad again."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (1592).

items.title: Quiz Q#191 · Thomas Kyd
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Kyd
items.stem: Which seminal play by Thomas Kyd, featuring the Ghost of Andrea and Revenge as choral observers, became the most influential and frequently performed revenge drama of the Elizabethan age?
items.explanation: The Spanish Tragedy (1592) established the conventions of Senecan Elizabethan tragedy, directly inspiring Shakespeare's Hamlet.

items.title: Quiz Q#192 · Thomas Lodge
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Lodge
items.stem: In which 1590 pastoral romance by Thomas Lodge does young Rosader flee into the Forest of Arden and woo Rosalynde, who is disguised as the pageboy Ganymede?
items.explanation: Rosalynde: Euphues Golden Legacy (1590) by Thomas Lodge provided the entire plot and character roster for Shakespeare's As You Like It.

items.title: Quiz Q#193 · Thomas Lodge
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Lodge
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Love in my bosom like a bee"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Lodge's Rosalynde (1590).

items.title: Quiz Q#194 · Thomas Lodge
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Lodge
items.stem: Which 1590 euphuistic prose romance by Thomas Lodge, written during a voyage to the Canary Islands and the Azores, was dramatized by William Shakespeare as As You Like It?
items.explanation: Lodge's Rosalynde (1590) was directly adapted by Shakespeare into As You Like It, with Rosader becoming Orlando and Rosalynde becoming Rosalind.

items.title: Quiz Q#195 · Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville
items.stem: In which 1561 play by Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville does King Gorboduc divide his British realm between his sons Ferrex and Porrex, provoking civil war and the destruction of the royal line?
items.explanation: Gorboduc (1561), performed at the Inner Temple and Whitehall, is universally recognized as the first regular English tragedy in blank verse.

items.title: Quiz Q#196 · Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The silent night that brings the quiet pause"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville's Gorboduc (1565).

items.title: Quiz Q#197 · Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville
items.stem: Which 1561 Senecan tragedy by Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville, also published under the title Ferrex and Porrex, utilized dumb shows and moral choruses to warn Queen Elizabeth about an unsettled royal succession?
items.explanation: Gorboduc (1561/65) used classical Senecan dramatic conventions and the medium of blank verse to deliver a political warning on the dangers of disputed royal succession.

items.title: Quiz Q#198 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Some books are to be tasted."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Francis Bacon's Essays (1597, enlarged 1612 and 1625).

items.title: Quiz Q#199 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Which landmark collection of aphoristic prose by Francis Bacon grew from 10 essays in 1597 to 38 in 1612 and 58 in the definitive 1625 edition, subtitled 'Counsels, Civil and Moral'?
items.explanation: Francis Bacon's Essays (1597, 1612, 1625) introduced the essay form from Montaigne into English, characterized by terse, pithy, and pragmatic moral reflections.

items.title: Quiz Q#200 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem: In Francis Bacon's utopian fable New Atlantis, what is the name of the state-sponsored scientific research college established to study nature 'for the relief of man's estate'?
items.explanation: Solomon's House (the College of the Six Days' Works) in Bacon's New Atlantis (1626) envisioned modern collaborative scientific research, inspiring the founding of the Royal Society in 1660.

items.title: Quiz Q#201 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"God bless thee, my son."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Francis Bacon's New Atlantis (1626).

items.title: Quiz Q#202 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Which unfinished utopian narrative by Francis Bacon, published posthumously in 1626 by William Rawley, describes the discovery of the hidden Pacific island of Bensalem and its scientific academy?
items.explanation: New Atlantis (1626) portrayed Bensalem's Christian-humanist society and Solomon's House, expressing Bacon's vision of scientific conquest over nature.

items.title: Quiz Q#203 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Which 1605 philosophical treatise dedicated to King James I categorizes human knowledge according to the three faculties of the rational soul: History (Memory), Poesy (Imagination), and Philosophy (Reason)?
items.explanation: The Advancement of Learning (1605) by Francis Bacon surveyed the contemporary state of scientific knowledge and proposed systematic educational reform.

items.title: Quiz Q#204 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Ill discoverers that think there is no land."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Francis Bacon's The Advancement of Learning (1605).

items.title: Quiz Q#205 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Which philosophical work by Francis Bacon, published in English in 1605 and later expanded into Latin as De Augmentis Scientiarum in 1623, served as the opening division of his Great Instauration?
items.explanation: The Advancement of Learning (1605) surveyed human learning and formed Part I of Bacon's grand project, the Instauratio Magna.

items.title: Quiz Q#206 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Nature to be commanded must be obeyed."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Francis Bacon's Novum Organum (1620).

items.title: Quiz Q#207 · Francis Bacon
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Which 1620 philosophical work by Francis Bacon, serving as Part II of the Instauratio Magna, outlines the inductive scientific method and formulates the famous doctrine of the Four Idols of the Mind?
items.explanation: Novum Organum (1620) introduced Bacon's inductive logic to replace Aristotle's Organon, classifying intellectual fallacies into Idols of the Tribe, Cave, Market-place, and Theatre.

items.title: Quiz Q#208 · Michael Drayton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Michael Drayton
items.stem: Which Elizabethan sonnet sequence by Michael Drayton contains the celebrated Sonnet 61 opening with the lines: 'Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part; / Nay, I have done, you get no more of me'?
items.explanation: Michael Drayton's Idea (first published as Ideas Mirrour in 1594, revised in 1619) includes the famous dramatic parting sonnet 'Since there's no help'.

items.title: Quiz Q#209 · Michael Drayton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Michael Drayton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Shake hands for ever, cancel all our vows."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Michael Drayton's Idea (1594).

items.title: Quiz Q#210 · Michael Drayton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Michael Drayton
items.stem: Which sonnet sequence by Michael Drayton, continually revised from its 1594 inception as Ideas Mirrour until its final 1619 collection, celebrated his lifelong devotion to Anne Goodere?
items.explanation: Drayton's Idea sequence documented his courtship of Anne Goodere, demonstrating dramatic colloquialism that anticipated the Metaphysical poets.

items.title: Quiz Q#211 · Michael Drayton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Michael Drayton
items.stem: Which monumental topographical poem by Michael Drayton, running to 15,000 alexandrine lines across 30 'Songs', systematically describes the rivers, mountains, forests, and antiquities of England and Wales?
items.explanation: Poly-Olbion (1612/1622) is Michael Drayton's chorographical epic celebrating the landscape, folklore, and history of Britain.

items.title: Quiz Q#212 · Michael Drayton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Michael Drayton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Thou Genius of the place."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Michael Drayton's Poly-Olbion (1612).

items.title: Quiz Q#213 · Michael Drayton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Michael Drayton
items.stem: Which ambitious topographical epic by Michael Drayton was published in two volumes (1612 and 1622) featuring elaborate engraved county maps by William Hole and antiquarian illustrations by John Selden?
items.explanation: Poly-Olbion (1612/22) is Drayton's 'chorographical description of all the tracts, rivers, mountains, forests, and other parts of this renowned isle of Great Britain'.

items.title: Quiz Q#214 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: In Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, which Wittenberg scholar sells his soul to Lucifer in exchange for twenty-four years of magical power and worldly knowledge?
items.explanation: Doctor Faustus is the tragic protagonist of Marlowe's drama (1604/1616), whose hubristic quest for forbidden power culminates in his terrifying midnight damnation.

items.title: Quiz Q#215 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Hell hath no limits, nor is circumscribed."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (1604 (A text), 1616 (B text)).

items.title: Quiz Q#216 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Which tragic drama by Christopher Marlowe survives in two distinct early versions—the shorter 'A-Text' of 1604 and the longer, more theatrical 'B-Text' of 1616?
items.explanation: Marlowe's Doctor Faustus exists in two primary textual authorities: the 1604 Quarto (A-Text) and the expanded 1616 Quarto (B-Text).

items.title: Quiz Q#217 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: In Christopher Marlowe's history play Edward II, which English monarch is deposed and brutally murdered at Berkeley Castle after alienating his barons through his infatuation with Piers Gaveston?
items.explanation: Edward II (1594) by Christopher Marlowe dramatizes the tragic fall and horrific murder of King Edward II, provoked by his defiance of the English nobility.

items.title: Quiz Q#218 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The mightiest kings have had their minions."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Christopher Marlowe's Edward II (1594).

items.title: Quiz Q#219 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Which 1594 play by Christopher Marlowe, performed by Pembroke's Men, pioneered the Elizabethan history play by focusing on political tragedy, favoritism, and the downfall of Mortimer and the King?
items.explanation: Edward II (1594) was Marlowe's mature history play, establishing psychological depth in historical drama that directly influenced Shakespeare's Richard II.

items.title: Quiz Q#220 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: In Christopher Marlowe's mythological epyllion Hero and Leander, who is the lovely priestess of Venus at Sestos whose beauty captivates the swimming youth of Abydos?
items.explanation: Hero is the priestess of Venus in Marlowe's unfinished erotic epyllion Hero and Leander (1598), later completed by George Chapman.

items.title: Quiz Q#221 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Where both deliberate, the love is slight."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Christopher Marlowe's Hero and Leander (1598).

items.title: Quiz Q#222 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Which erotic narrative poem left incomplete at Christopher Marlowe's death in 1593 was published in 1598 with a four-sestiad continuation written by George Chapman?
items.explanation: Hero and Leander (1598) was left as two sestiads by Marlowe upon his death; George Chapman completed the poem with four additional sestiads.

items.title: Quiz Q#223 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: In which groundbreaking two-part tragedy by Christopher Marlowe does a Scythian shepherd rise by ruthless military conquest to become emperor of the world, proclaiming himself the 'Scourge of God'?
items.explanation: Tamburlaine the Great (1590) by Marlowe established blank verse as the dominant meter of the Elizabethan public theater through Edward Alleyn's mighty performances.

items.title: Quiz Q#224 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"And ride in triumph through Persepolis."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine (1590).

items.title: Quiz Q#225 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Which 1587-88 stage triumph by Christopher Marlowe popularized 'Marlowe's mighty line'—sonorous, unrhymed blank verse—across two five-act plays celebrating world conquest?
items.explanation: Tamburlaine the Great revolutionized Elizabethan theatrical verse with its sweeping rhetorical cadence, famously praised by Ben Jonson as 'Marlowe's mighty line'.

items.title: Quiz Q#226 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: In Christopher Marlowe's The Jew of Malta, which Machiavellian merchant hoards 'infinite riches in a little room' and poisons a convent of nuns after the Governor seizes his wealth?
items.explanation: Barabas is the villain-hero of Marlowe's The Jew of Malta (c. 1589/1633), whose savage revenge against Christians and Turks ends in a boiling cauldron.

items.title: Quiz Q#227 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Infinite riches in a little room."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Christopher Marlowe's The Jew of Malta (1633).

items.title: Quiz Q#228 · Christopher Marlowe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Which cynical revenge tragedy by Christopher Marlowe opens with a prologue spoken by 'Machevil' and features Barabas, his slave Ithamore, and Governor Ferneze in a battle of Mediterranean realpolitik?
items.explanation: The Jew of Malta opens with Machiavelli's ghost declaring 'I count religion but a childish toy', setting the tone for Marlowe's dark commercial satire.

items.title: Quiz Q#229 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In which narrative poem by William Shakespeare does the goddess of love passionately woo an indifferent youth who is subsequently killed by a wild boar on a hunt?
items.explanation: Venus and Adonis (1593) is Shakespeare's Ovidian erotic narrative poem in sesta rima stanzas, dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton.

items.title: Quiz Q#230 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Love is a spirit all compact of fire."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis (1593 (Quarto)).

items.title: Quiz Q#231 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which narrative poem by William Shakespeare, dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton in 1593 as 'the first heir of my invention', became his first published literary work?
items.explanation: Venus and Adonis (1593) was Shakespeare's first printed work, published during the London plague closures of 1592-1594 by Richard Field.

items.title: Quiz Q#232 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In which Shakespearean tragedy do the teenage heirs of the feuding Capulet and Montague households fall into secret love, ending in their double suicide in the family monument?
items.explanation: Romeo and Juliet (1597) dramatizes the doomed romantic love of the 'star-crossed lovers' against the violent backdrop of Verona.

items.title: Quiz Q#233 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"A pair of star-crossed lovers take their life."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet (1597 (Quarto 1), 1599 (Quarto 2), 1623 (First Folio)).

items.title: Quiz Q#234 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which tragedy of William Shakespeare opens with a fourteen-line prologue in sonnet form introducing the ancient grudge between 'two households, both alike in dignity / In fair Verona'?
items.explanation: Romeo and Juliet famously opens with a Shakespearean sonnet spoken by the Chorus to set the dramatic scene and foreshadow the lovers' death.

items.title: Quiz Q#235 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, which mischievous fairy spirit mistakenly anoints the sleeping Lysander's eyes with the juice of 'love-in-idleness'?
items.explanation: Puck (Robin Goodfellow) is Oberon's jester in A Midsummer Night's Dream (1600), whose magic transforms Bottom with an ass's head and confuses the Athenian lovers.

items.title: Quiz Q#236 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Lord, what fools these mortals be!"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio)).

items.title: Quiz Q#237 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In which Shakespearean comedy do the craftsmen ('rude mechanicals') rehearse and perform the farcical interlude of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' for the wedding of Duke Theseus and Hippolyta?
items.explanation: A Midsummer Night's Dream features the comic theatrical interlude performed by Nick Bottom, Peter Quince, and their fellow workingmen.

items.title: Quiz Q#238 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 1, which prince frequents the Boar's Head Tavern in Eastcheap with Falstaff before redeeming himself by slaying Harry Hotspur at the Battle of Shrewsbury?
items.explanation: Prince Hal (the future King Henry V) promises to 'imitate the sun' by casting off his tavern misbehavior in Henry IV, Part 1.

items.title: Quiz Q#239 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The better part of valour is discretion."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 1 (1598 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio)).

items.title: Quiz Q#240 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which Shakespearean history play features Sir John Falstaff's famous 'catechism on honour' and depicts the northern rebellion led by Henry Percy (Hotspur) against King Henry IV?
items.explanation: Henry IV, Part 1 (1598) balances historical civil rebellion with the tavern comedy of Falstaff, Poins, and Prince Hal.

items.title: Quiz Q#241 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, which Jewish moneylender demands the forfeiture of a pound of Antonio's flesh under strict bond before being defeated in court by Portia?
items.explanation: Shylock is the complex Venetian moneylender in The Merchant of Venice (1600), delivering the speech 'Hath not a Jew eyes?'.

items.title: Quiz Q#242 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The quality of mercy is not strained."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio)).

items.title: Quiz Q#243 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which Shakespearean comedy combines the romantic casket lottery at Belmont with the legal courtroom contest over a 'pound of flesh' before the Duke of Venice?
items.explanation: The Merchant of Venice features Portia disguising herself as the young lawyer Balthazar to rescue Antonio from Shylock's forfeiture claim.

items.title: Quiz Q#244 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing, which quick-witted heroine engages in a 'merry war' of intellect and insults with Benedick before being tricked into mutual love?
items.explanation: Beatrice is the sharp-tongued, independent heroine of Much Ado About Nothing (1600) who famously commands Benedick to 'Kill Claudio'.

items.title: Quiz Q#245 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing (1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio)).

items.title: Quiz Q#246 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which Shakespearean comedy set in Messina depicts Don John's slandering of the innocent Hero at the altar and the comedic blundering of Constable Dogberry and the Watch?
items.explanation: Much Ado About Nothing (1600) weaves together the dark villainy of Don John with the brilliant comedic courtship of Beatrice and Benedick.

items.title: Quiz Q#247 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare's Roman tragedy Julius Caesar, which idealistic patrician joins the conspiracy of Cassius on the Ides of March, declaring: 'Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more'?
items.explanation: Marcus Brutus is the conflicted moral center of Julius Caesar (1599), praised after his suicide by Mark Antony as 'the noblest Roman of them all'.

items.title: Quiz Q#248 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In which Shakespearean tragedy does Mark Antony deliver the famous funeral oration beginning 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears', inciting the Roman mob against Caesar's assassins?
items.explanation: Julius Caesar (1599) features Antony's masterpiece of political rhetoric over Caesar's corpse in the Forum, turning public sentiment against the conspirators.

items.title: Quiz Q#249 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In which Shakespearean tragedy does the Prince of Denmark feign madness ('an antic disposition') to avenge his father's murder by his uncle King Claudius?
items.explanation: Hamlet (c. 1601/03) is Shakespeare's greatest tragedy of revenge, philosophical hesitation, and mortality.

items.title: Quiz Q#250 · William Shakespeare
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which Shakespearean tragedy features the dramatic device of 'The Mousetrap' ('The Murder of Gonzago'), staged before the royal court of Elsinore to 'catch the conscience of the King'?
items.explanation: In Hamlet, Prince Hamlet commissions the traveling players to perform a dramatization of his father's poisoning to confirm Claudius's guilt.
